storyboard.addedInformation: The alarm clock makes the interrupted cycle visible; the narration only describes being jolted.
storyboard.claim: Blue light suppresses melatonin, shifts the wake surge to the night, and the alarm cuts the shortened cycle short.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An exhausted office worker jolting upright in a dark bedroom as an alarm clock rings beside the bed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the blue-light setup from beats 117-119: the light lied that it was noon, now the bill arrives.

storyboard.addedInformation: Names the 2012 discovery as a named system the viewer can anchor the next beats to.
storyboard.claim: Cutting sleep short is devastating because of the glymphatic system, discovered in 2012.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sleep physician pausing mid-explanation, finger raised, as if introducing a breakthrough finding.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the alarm cut the cycle short: now the question of why that cut matters.

storyboard.addedInformation: Stages the daytime brain as a working machine too busy to clean, setting up the sleep contrast.
storyboard.claim: Firing brain cells burn energy all day and produce metabolic waste.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The sleep physician explaining while tapping his temple: a busy working brain with no time to clean.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Zooms into the mechanism just named: what the waste is and when it piles up.

storyboard.addedInformation: The worried face marks these proteins as dangerous, which the words alone underplay.
storyboard.claim: The waste includes toxic proteins like amyloid beta, and the awake brain is too busy to clear them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The physician's face turning grave as he names the toxic buildup inside an overworked head.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the waste from the previous beat: toxic proteins left sitting because the brain is busy.

callout.text: THE BRAIN SHRINKS TO MAKE ROOM

storyboard.addedInformation: The raised finger plus startled face sells the counterintuitive shrink claim without any diagram.
storyboard.claim: In deep sleep the brain cells literally shrink, opening gaps between them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The physician pointing upward in surprise, driving home the strange image of shrinking cells.
storyboard.onScreenText: THE BRAIN SHRINKS TO MAKE ROOM
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The turn: from the waking problem to what deep sleep physically does about it.

storyboard.addedInformation: The sweeping gesture traces the fluid's path through the opened gaps.
storyboard.claim: The opened gaps let cerebrospinal fluid rush in between the cells.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The physician sweeping his hand through the air, tracing fluid flooding into the brain's opened spaces.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Direct continuation: the gaps just opened, now the fluid floods them.

storyboard.addedInformation: Water reads literally here as the flushing fluid itself, the subject of the sentence.
storyboard.claim: The fluid washes through the brain, flushing the toxic proteins out toward the liver.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flowing water washing through, carrying the waste away with it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The payoff of the flood: the rush becomes a wash that carries toxins out.

storyboard.addedInformation: The slumped insomniac embodies the uncleaned street: a dirty, uncleared head at 3 a.m.
storyboard.claim: Like a 3 a.m. street sweeper, deep sleep cleans the brain; too little sleep leaves the streets dirty.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The exhausted worker slumped on the edge of the bed in the small hours, head clouded and uncleared.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Metaphor lands on the body: the municipal sweeper image becomes one sleepless person.

storyboard.addedInformation: Stages the double penalty on one concerned expert face: dirty streets plus unsaved memories.
storyboard.claim: Built-up toxins cloud cognition, and lost REM means the day's learning never encodes into memory.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The physician grave-faced, one hand at his temple for the clouded mind, the other closing like a book that never got saved.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the dirty streets to their two costs: clouded thinking and unencoded memory.

storyboard.addedInformation: The slump plus the callout makes the sludge claim bodily: this is what five hours feels like at dawn.
storyboard.claim: Five hours of sleep means waking with a sludge-filled brain and nothing learned saved.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The worker collapsed over the bedside at dawn, head heavy with sludge, the day's lessons spilled unsaved.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The double whammy lands on the sufferer: yesterday's toxins plus yesterday's lost learning.

storyboard.addedInformation: Two slumped figures side by side show the impairment is shared, not one man's flaw.
storyboard.claim: You start the day cognitively impaired, yet humans are the most adaptable species.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The drained worker slumped beside the journalist at dawn: two impaired brains, one posing the adaptation question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sums up the damage, then pivots: if we are so adaptable, why can't we adjust?

callout.text: CAN WE EVOLVE TO NEED LESS?

storyboard.addedInformation: Johann voicing it as a genuine question keeps it curious rather than a boast.
storyboard.claim: If we survived ice ages and famines, perhaps we can evolve to need less sleep.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The journalist asking it straight, open-handed: survivors of ice ages questioning their own limits.
storyboard.onScreenText: CAN WE EVOLVE TO NEED LESS?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The challenge sharpened: ice ages and migrations offered as evidence we could adapt.

storyboard.addedInformation: The cup in hand with a flat neutral face shows the hollow version of fine: wired, not rested.
storyboard.claim: Executives who feel fine on five hours plus coffee are not adapting; biologically they are breaking.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The worker clutching a coffee cup with a blank wired stare: functioning, not adapting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the adaptation question with the coffee-cup rebuttal: surviving is not adapting.

storyboard.addedInformation: The physician's steady explainer pose grounds the chemistry before the cork metaphor lands.
storyboard.claim: All day the brain builds adenosine, which creates rising sleep pressure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The physician calmly explaining, pressing a palm down like pressure steadily building through the day.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the coffee boast to the chemistry underneath: what tiredness actually is.

storyboard.addedInformation: The flow strips the cork metaphor to its mechanics: the pressure exists whether or not you feel it.
storyboard.claim: Caffeine does not remove adenosine; it plugs the receptors like tape over a warning light.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The physician pointing at a simple chain: adenosine building, caffeine plugging the way through, and the sleep pressure still climbing behind it.
storyboard.onScreenText: Caffeine plugs the receptors, so the pressure stays
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Mechanizes the previous beat: the pressure named there is now shown being masked, not removed.

storyboard.addedInformation: The cup plus the uneasy face stages self-deception: the engine overheats behind a taped-over light.
storyboard.claim: The engine still overheats and adenosine still builds; caffeine only hides the feeling for hours.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The worker gripping the cup with dawning worry: the warning light is taped over but the engine still burns.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The cork's consequence on the drinker: masked signal, unmasked damage.

storyboard.addedInformation: The physician's anger reframes exhaustion from lifestyle choice to extraction strategy.
storyboard.claim: The economy relies on sleep-depriving people to squeeze out more labor, so exhaustion is profitable.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The physician speaking with stern urgency beside the exhausted worker he is describing: a system that trades sleep for hours.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Widens from the cup to the economy: your hidden tiredness is someone else's margin.

storyboard.addedInformation: The slumped desk worker living all three lapses makes them symptoms, not character flaws.
storyboard.claim: Forgotten names, lost trains of thought, paragraphs reread four times: the attentional failures of exhaustion.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The worker slumped at the office desk mid-sentence, the thought visibly slipping away.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The profit motive itemized: this is what the sleep-deprived workday actually looks like.

storyboard.addedInformation: The sad but unashamed slump lifts blame: failure reframed as fallout.
storyboard.claim: These lapses are not personal failures but the predictable biological fallout of a system that profits from wakefulness.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The worker bowed but unashamed: a good brain broken by a system, not a weak person.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Absolves the worker just shown failing: the lapses were evidence, this is the verdict.

storyboard.addedInformation: The phone gripped while braced shows saturation plus vigilance in one posture.
storyboard.claim: The commons' restorative waters are dammed up, so toxin-saturated brains brace for the next interruption instead of recharging.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The worker sitting rigid, hands empty and open on his knees, braced for the next interruption instead of resting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From verdict to image: the dammed waters leave everyone permanently braced.

storyboard.addedInformation: A new expert face marks the chapter turn from sleep to reading.
storyboard.claim: Constant interruption has mutated how we process information: the fourth structural cause is the skimming brain.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reading researcher announcing the turn: from sleepless brains to skimming ones.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Bridge beat: sleep damage done, the next mutation in how we read is named.

storyboard.addedInformation: The winter walk stages the detox as a physical journey to a far edge.
storyboard.claim: To see the mutation clearly, follow Johann to wintry Provincetown on the tip of Cape Cod.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The journalist walking a quiet grey winter street toward the far tip of the cape.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Leaves the lab for the field: the argument moves to a cold coastal town.

storyboard.addedInformation: The solitary walk against a vast grey backdrop shows detox as quiet endurance.
storyboard.claim: Weeks into his digital detox, Johann walks beside a gray, vast ocean in the quiet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The journalist walking alone under a flat cold sky, the vast gray ocean beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Arrives fully: the quiet vastness around him mirrors the detox experiment.

storyboard.addedInformation: The book icon reads literally as the shop's promise: printed pages waiting inside.
storyboard.claim: He steps off the quiet street into Tim's used books as the bell jingles.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The journalist pushing into a bookshop doorway, books stacked inside, a bell ringing above the door.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The walk ends at a door: from the grey outdoors to the sanctuary within.

storyboard.addedInformation: The held book plus the deep inhale face makes the smell itself visible.
storyboard.claim: Inside, a cozy narrow space smells of old, degrading paper: the best smell, a sanctuary.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The journalist lifting an old volume and breathing in its scent, enclosed by close shelves.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Inside the shop: the doorway's promise becomes paper, scent, and shelter.

storyboard.addedInformation: Johann's delighted gestures toward the shelves establish what surrounds the bookseller before her confession undercuts it.
storyboard.claim: The young bookseller is smart and articulate, ringed by history's greatest literary masterpieces.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The journalist chatting warmly, gesturing at towering shelves of great books all around the counter.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Meets the human center of the sanctuary: brilliance surrounded by greatness.

callout.text: SHE ONLY GETS THROUGH ONE CHAPTER

storyboard.addedInformation: The single book plus the fallen face stages abundance that cannot be used.
storyboard.claim: Tolstoy, Baldwin, Austen on the shelves, yet she confesses her brain gives out after a single chapter.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A single open book in the journalist's hands as he listens: masterpieces everywhere on the shelves, and one chapter is all she gets through.
storyboard.onScreenText: SHE ONLY GETS THROUGH ONE CHAPTER
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The sanctuary cracks: surrounded by masterpieces, she admits she cannot read them.

storyboard.addedInformation: The slumped reader with time and desire but no engine shows the tragedy is cognitive, not motivational.
storyboard.claim: She has the time, the shop, and the desire, yet her cognitive engine sputters out after twenty pages.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A reader slumped over an open book after a few pages: willing, unhurried, and stalled.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens the confession: it is not circumstance that fails her, but the engine itself.

storyboard.addedInformation: The pointed finger turns McLuhan's slogan into an accusation aimed at the screen habit.
storyboard.claim: The medium is the message: ten hours a day of screen reading physically trains the brain how to read.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The researcher pointing firmly: the screen habit itself rewiring the reader behind her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From one stalled reader to the law behind her: the medium trained her brain.

storyboard.addedInformation: The phone in hand reads literally as the modern screen doing the training.
storyboard.claim: Screens train us to scan, skip, and extract instead of reading.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A reader skewered to a glowing smartphone, eyes flicking across it, hunting rather than reading.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the training in action: the wiring described becomes thumbs and flicking eyes.

storyboard.addedInformation: The phone plus the scanning gaze stages the top-left-to-bottom-right habit the studies tracked.
storyboard.claim: Nobody reads a web page top-left to bottom-right; eye-tracking studies prove we dart and skim.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader's gaze darting across the phone screen, hunting the page instead of following it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Invites the viewer to catch themselves: watch how your own eyes move.

storyboard.addedInformation: The jabbing finger traces the F shape: headline, drop, bullet, margin scan, bail.
storyboard.claim: Screen reading follows an F pattern: headline, drop, bullet, keyword scan, then bail.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A finger tracing a sharp F across the air: headline across, drop down, scan, gone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the shape of the darting just shown: the F pattern.

storyboard.addedInformation: The hungry grip on the phone plus darting eyes shows the hit-seeking the narration describes.
storyboard.claim: Eyes dart for the quickest dopamine hit, and years of it thicken those neural pathways until paper reads the same way.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader clawed onto the phone, eyes flicking hungrily for the next hit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the F: the eyes are not reading, they are hunting hits.

storyboard.addedInformation: The book clutched with a grieving face stages a biological capacity collapsing, not a habit slipping.
storyboard.claim: We are collapsing our own biological ability to read deeply, even on printed paper.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The researcher clutching a printed book with grief: the deep-reading capacity itself crumbling.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The sentence on the habit: the hunting has now broken paper reading too.

storyboard.addedInformation: The expert's level explainer pose introduces the fragility: reading was never hardwired.
storyboard.claim: Unlike vision or language, humans have no genetic reading center; reading is not what we were born to do.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The researcher explaining plainly: a brain with no built-in reading slot, learning it from scratch.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grounds the collapse in biology: deep reading was never guaranteed by our genes.

storyboard.addedInformation: The elder expert beside the eager teen stages learning as rewiring across generations.
storyboard.claim: Every child learning to read must physically repurpose visual and language circuits and wire them together.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The researcher guiding the teenager, tracing new connections being wired across a young mind.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the delicate wiring that was never hardwired: built by hand, circuit by circuit.

storyboard.addedInformation: The worried face marks plasticity as danger: the same flexibility that builds the circuit lets the screen unbuild it.
storyboard.claim: Because the circuit is so plastic, training it for fast screen extraction drains the stamina for linear books.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The researcher grave-faced: a once-sturdy reading circuit thinning under screen training.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The plasticity warning: what the screen trains, the book loses.

storyboard.addedInformation: The researcher's citing gesture presents Norway as evidence, not opinion.
storyboard.claim: Norwegian researchers tested screen inferiority, and the findings are definitive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The researcher presenting the study like evidence: Norway's verdict on screens versus paper.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From mechanism to proof: a named study to test the plasticity claim.

storyboard.addedInformation: The held printed book against the described screen half stages the controlled comparison.
storyboard.claim: Half the students read a text on screen, half read the exact same text on printed paper.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The researcher holding up the printed half of the experiment: same words, two media, one fair test.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lays out the experiment both halves will be judged by.

storyboard.addedInformation: The teen's slump over the result makes screen inferiority a personal loss, not a statistic.
storyboard.claim: The screen readers consistently scored lower, losing the equivalent of two-thirds of a year's comprehension.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The teenager slumped over his results: the screen-taught reader falling behind.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The verdict lands on the young: same text, lower score, two-thirds of a year gone.
